newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka lowers reserve ratios to boost economy.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka lowers reserve ratios to boost economy.

text.p: Sri Lanka is trying to boost economic growth to six percent in 1997 by cutting bank reserve ratios to help lower corporate borrowing rates, but bankers said on Wednesday the move could backfire and fuel inflation.

The Central Bank said on Monday it was reducing the reserve requirements of commercial banks by two percent to 12 percent in a move that would improve market liquidity by 5.3 billion rupees ($91.3 million).
Sri Lanka last relaxed monetary policy in January by cutting the reserve ratio by one percent to 14 percent and permitting exporters to borrow in foreign currency.
The two rapid cuts in reserve ratios drew a mixed response from Sri Lankan bankers who say the excess liquidity could easily end up being used for consumption and fuel inflation.
"Banks which were drowning in short term funds after the first cut may be forced to lend to consumers after the second cut," said a Commercial Bank dealer.
Annualised inflation was 16.7 percent in February compared to 15.9 percent for the whole of 1996. Analysts project inflation at 13 percent in 1997, but the government says it will be a single digit.
Treasury officials are confident that budgetary targets can be met in 1997.

"Revenue generation has been good so far this year, and we have set conservative targets for privatisation inflows at five billion rupees," P.B. Jayasundera, treasury deputy secretary and chairman of the Public Enterprise Reform Commission (PERC) told Reuters.

The PERC, which oversees privatisations, is currently working on shedding 35 percent and management of state telecommunications monopoly Sri Lanka Telecom, and 40 percent and management in the national carrier Airlanka.

"The privatisation process is gathering momentum and money growth is showing signs of stabilising at about 16 percent which is conducive to a six percent GDP (gross domestic product) growth and single digit inflation," Jayasundera said.
The recent cut in the reserve ratio should therefore provide the shot in the arm necessary to boost economic growth which is already showing signs of improving, Jayasundera said.

"Using low rates to try to trigger off investment which can boost growth that will ultimately reduce the budget deficit is not a bad strategy," Ajit Gunewardene, director of Colombo blue chip John Keells Holdings told Reuters.
"If this means that we can borrow at 15 percent what we have been borrowing at 18 (percent), we will definitely look at gearing more aggressively," Gunewardena said.

The country's GDP growth was restrained in 1995 and 1996 by a huge budget deficit mostly due to increased government spending to modernise the military, which is fighting Tamil Tiger rebels in a 14-year old civil war.

GDP growth in 1996, also hit by a severe drought, is expected to stand at four percent, down from 5.5 percent in 1995. The 1996 budget deficit is forecast at about nine percent of GDP compared to 8.4 percent in 1995.

"The move to hold rates low is also based on the assumption government borrowings will not rise and privatisation proceeds will flow through," said Kumar Abayanayaka, chief executive of Sampath Bank Ltd. At Tuesday's auction, the day after the cut in reserve ratios, the 12-month benchmark Treasury Bill rate was at 13.48 percent, down from a 1996 high of 19.05 percent in January last year.
The government also floated two-year Treasury Bonds for the first time in March this year.
